title: Reading, closed
hookLine: a season of sources read yourself
tomorrow: a 7am studio call. can a morning practice survive that?

lines: THE ONE THAT TALKS TO YOU?
OR THE ONE THE MONKS CHOOSE?
cards: Packing for six weeks away is a quiz on who you are: one bag, and every book has to earn its spot. Mai has room for one. Ông says take the one that talks to you. Her mom says take the one the monks would choose.
It's the question this whole season of reading has been circling. You've read the sources yourself, line by line, from the suttas to the songs.
So who gets the final say on what they mean: your own ear, or the people who've walked the path longer?

teach.h: THE KALAMAS: WHOM DO WE BELIEVE?
teach.b: Both sides have a sutta, and they deserve to be heard. The first view: trust your own testing.
The Kalamas, a town confused by visiting teachers who each praised their own doctrine and knocked the others, asked the Buddha whom to believe.
He told them not to go by report, or tradition, or scripture, or respect for a teacher alone.
When you know for yourselves that something leads to harm, let it go; when it leads to welfare and happiness, take it up.
Near the end of his life, in the Rhys Davids translation, he told Ananda, "be ye lamps unto yourselves." The second view: read with those who've gone further.
The same Kalama talk has a second test inside it: notice what the wise praise and what they blame.

teach.h: A LAMP, AND THE TRUTH AS REFUGE.
teach.b: The lamp line comes with a partner too: hold to the truth, the dhamma, as your lamp and refuge.
Zen and Tibetan schools speak of the teaching passed from teacher to student, and a temple's readings are chosen by the people who kept them.
So a reader on this path stands between two things: your own testing, and the long company of those who tested before you. That's what this season was for.
You read them yourself. Not alone, and not against anyone. Yourself.

how: Buddhist schools balance personal study and testing with a teacher's guidance: students read texts on their own, with a teacher, or in a study group, and practice what they read to see what it does.

o: taking the texts in yourself, tested, in good company
letting a teacher decide which books you may open
finishing every book on a list before moving on

games.q: two views, one path — tap the pairs.
p: what leads to harm, what to welfare
whose praise and blame you weigh

s: the Kalama Sutta says to believe whatever feels right to you
it says know for yourselves what leads to harm or welfare, and also notice what the wise praise and blame.
the Buddha told Ananda to be a lamp unto himself
in Rhys Davids's words, be ye lamps unto yourselves, with the truth as lamp and refuge too.
in Buddhism a text only counts if a teacher hands it to you
schools weigh it differently: some stress testing it yourself, some a teacher's guidance, and the two can go together.

games.q: a friend says: 'the Buddha told the Kalamas not to trust scripture, so i'll skip the texts and go by my gut.' give the other side's best case.
o: the same talk says weigh what the wise praise and blame, not just your gut
scripture always outranks experience in Buddhism, so the gut doesn't count
your gut is all the Buddha meant, so there isn't another side
games.why: the Kalama talk has two tests in it: what you know for yourself, and what the wise praise and blame. both views can quote it.

practice: Bring to mind the text from this season that spoke loudest, and write one line of it by hand, from memory if you can. Sit for two minutes with the page in front of you. If someone once read it with you, let them be in the room too.

wordCard.voice: Reading: the season's last word. Not a pile of books, but a habit: testing what you read, in good company.

orig.note: Pali: a lamp, and also an island. The word behind 'be ye lamps unto yourselves'; some readers hear 'islands'.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: you read them yourself, and you weren't the first to. Season closed.
